content.title: Canada Just Made It Easier for Americans to Get Citizenship—What to Know
content.text: It is easier than ever to become a Canadian citizen if you have the right family history. Canada recently expanded citizenship eligibility, extending citizenship by descent beyond just the first generation, according to the government. The new rule, Bill C-3, An Act to Amend the Citizenship Act, went into effect in December. The government said the new law was created with the goal "to extend citizenship by descent beyond the first-generation in a way that is more inclusive and protects the value of Canadian citizenship." “There's no limit on how many generations you can go back, as long as you can prove it,” Cassandra Fultz, a Canadian immigration consultant, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), adding it comes at a time many Americans are seeking to obtain second passports. In fact, the CBC reported some Americans have already taken advantage of the new opportunity. The new law also addresses what the government calls "lost Canadians," or "people who lost or never obtained citizenship because of certain outdated rules in earlier citizenship laws." To prove citizenship by descent, Fultz told the CBC the main documents people need are baptismal or birth certificates and marriage certificates to demonstrate potential name changes. Beyond citizenship by descent, adult transplants can become citizens of Canada by being permanent residents, living in Canada for three out of five years, filed any necessary income taxes in the country, and having an adequate knowledge of English or French, according to the government. Holding a Canadian passport can be powerful. The country's passport is currently ranked as the 7th most powerful in the world, providing visa-free access to more than 182 destinations, according to the Henley Passport Index. It is tied with Australia, Czechia, Latvia, New Zealand, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Conversely, the United States is currently ranked 10th on the list with visa-free access to 179 destinations. Beyond Canada, several other countries allow people to claim citizenship based on family history, including Spain, Ireland, Italy, and Poland. Others allow for citizenship by investment, like in Portugal and the Caribbean islands of St. Kitts and Nevis. In the U.S., Americans are able to become dual citizens, but the Department of State noted some countries may not recognize a traveler's U.S. nationality when they are traveling internationally and that may result in limited U.S. assistance while abroad. Dual U.S. citizens must also enter and exit the U.S. using their American passport.
